entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Count Michał Jerzy Wandalin Mniszech (1748–1806) was a Polish nobleman who played a significant role in the late 18th-century European nobility.

Mniszech was born into a prominent aristocratic family and served as a military officer during the Seven Years' War. He later became involved in the affairs of his family's estates and worked to modernize their agricultural practices.

His efforts contributed to the growth of the Mniszech family's economic influence, particularly in the region of Volhynia.

Mniszech died on March 14, 1806, at the age of 58.

He is remembered for his role in shaping the nobility of Poland during this period and his efforts to modernize agricultural practices in Eastern Europe.

entities.summary:
Count Michał Jerzy Wandalin Mniszech (1748–1806) was a prominent magnate and statesman of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, whose career spanned the tumultuous final decades leading to its complete dissolution. Born into the immensely wealthy Mniszech family at Vyshnivets, he inherited vast estates and significant political influence, positioning him as a key player in the intricate power struggles that defined 18th-century Central European politics. His trajectory from a trusted advisor to King Stanisław August Poniatowski to a controversial figure who aligned with the Targowica Confederation illuminates the deep internal divisions and external pressures that ultimately led to Poland's demise. Mniszech's life serves as a microcosm of the Polish nobility's struggle to adapt to Enlightenment ideals while grappling with the encroaching imperial ambitions of Russia, Prussia, and Austria.

Mniszech ascended through the Commonwealth's administrative ranks, becoming Grand Secretary of Lithuania in 1778 and Grand Marshal of the Crown in 1783, a powerful position responsible for the royal court and security. He initially supported King Stanisław August Poniatowski's reform efforts, including participation in the Permanent Council, an executive body designed to streamline governance. His personal wealth allowed him to be a lavish patron of the arts, accumulating a renowned library of over 15,000 volumes and sponsoring theatrical productions. However, his political loyalties shifted dramatically as the Commonwealth faced existential threats. He became a vocal opponent of the Constitution of 3 May 1791, viewing it as an infringement on noble liberties, and subsequently joined the pro-Russian Targowica Confederation in 1792, an act widely regarded as a betrayal that precipitated the Second Partition of Poland.
